classification.difficultyReason: Translate six supplied inequalities directly into rays or intervals, distinguishing open and closed endpoints.

questions.mappingNote: Question 1 requires graphing supplied real-number sets without algebraic manipulation; represent-inequalities-number-line is the directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Example 1 on PDF page 2 represents a strict boundary with an open circle and an included boundary with a closed circle, using a ray or a segment for the solution set. Page 3 continues the section with Example 2 before Exercise 4A.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate six supplied inequalities directly into rays or intervals, distinguishing open and closed endpoints.

classification.difficultyReason: Solve routine linear inequations, including pronumerals on both sides, and represent strict or inclusive bounds on number lines.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts directly assess solving linear inequalities and graphing their solutions. Parts a–d require one or two inverse operations; e and f first collect pronumeral terms. No part requires division by a negative coefficient.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 states that the same addition, subtraction, multiplication or division is applied to both sides, reversing the inequality for a negative multiplier or divisor. Example 1 solves linear inequations step by step, then graphs solutions using open or closed endpoints and rays or segments. Page 3 Example 2 applies the same algebraic operations in context.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Solve routine linear inequations, including pronumerals on both sides, and represent strict or inclusive bounds on number lines.

classification.difficultyReason: Routine linear inequations progress from negative coefficients to collecting variable terms on both sides; division by a negative reverses the inequality.

questions.mappingNote: Each part directly assesses solving a linear inequality. Parts a–c require one negative division; d–f also remove a constant; g–i collect variable terms before isolating x. No graph is requested.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 states that equal operations preserve an inequation except that multiplication or division by a negative reverses its sign. Example 1a collects variable terms, removes the constant, then divides by a negative. Page 3 Example 2 applies the same reversal.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Routine linear inequations progress from negative coefficients to collecting variable terms on both sides; division by a negative reverses the inequality.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply inverse operations to all three expressions in a double inequality and represent both endpoint conditions on a number line.

questions.mappingNote: Each assigned part requires solving a linear double inequality by addition, subtraction or positive division and graphing the resulting bounded interval. No negative division is necessary.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 states the same-operation rule and demonstrates applying operations to all three expressions of a double inequation in Example 1b. Its number line uses closed endpoints for included bounds; Example 1a demonstrates an open endpoint for an excluded bound.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply inverse operations to all three expressions in a double inequality and represent both endpoint conditions on a number line.

classification.difficultyReason: Solve compound linear inequalities with negative coefficients, reverse both inequality signs and express the endpoints using interval notation.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts directly assess solving double linear inequations using these algebraic operations. Interval notation is the explicitly requested final representation.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 states that multiplying or dividing by a negative reverses the inequality sign. Example 1b applies each operation to all three expressions of a double inequation and reverses both signs when dividing by a negative. Page 3 Example 2 reinforces the same reversal rule.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Solve compound linear inequalities with negative coefficients, reverse both inequality signs and express the endpoints using interval notation.

classification.difficultyReason: Clear numerical denominators, collect variable terms and reverse inequalities when dividing by negative coefficients, then express solutions in interval notation.

questions.mappingNote: Each part requires solving a linear inequality with numerical fractions. Interval notation is the explicit final response requirement, so it is a secondary skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 106 states that the same operations apply to both sides, with inequality reversal when multiplying or dividing by a negative. Example 1 demonstrates sequential algebraic operations and the reversal; Example 2 applies the same method.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Clear numerical denominators, collect variable terms and reverse inequalities when dividing by negative coefficients, then express solutions in interval notation.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret supplied line graphs to determine solution regions, then independently confirm both inequalities algebraically.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts directly assess linear inequalities; part a compares a line with the x-axis and part b compares the heights of two lines.
questions.methodNote: Apply the same algebraic operations to both sides, reversing the inequality when dividing by a negative. Interpret the supplied graphs before confirming algebraically.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Interpret supplied line graphs to determine solution regions, then independently confirm both inequalities algebraically.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct linear graphs and interpret vertical comparisons to solve inequalities.

questions.mappingNote: Solving linear inequalities is the most advanced directly assessed skill; graph construction supports the required graphical method.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 establishes inequality operations and number-line solutions; page 3 models practical linear inequations. Question 8 explicitly requires constructing and interpreting coordinate graphs, so the solutions use intercepts and relative graph heights.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct linear graphs and interpret vertical comparisons to solve inequalities.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate the relative heights of two lines into a strict inequality, then solve with fractional coefficients.

questions.mappingNote: Comparing the two line heights gives a linear inequation with the variable on both sides, directly assessing solving linear inequalities.
questions.methodNote: Apply the same algebraic operation to both sides of an inequation; reverse its sign when multiplying or dividing by a negative number.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate the relative heights of two lines into a strict inequality, then solve with fractional coefficients.

classification.difficultyReason: Connect a double inequality to three straight-line graphs, then transfer the graphical interpretation to two related inequalities.

questions.mappingNote: Question 10 combines the double-inequality method demonstrated in Example 1b with graphical comparison. Referenced Questions 4a and 5a are visible on source PDF page 3.
questions.methodNote: Apply the same algebraic operation throughout a double inequality; reverse both signs when dividing by a negative. Relate the resulting interval to the positions of straight-line graphs.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Connect a double inequality to three straight-line graphs, then transfer the graphical interpretation to two related inequalities.

classification.difficultyReason: Model monthly interest, solve two inequalities and interpret integer payment counts as calendar dates.

questions.mappingNote: Parts b and c directly assess solving linear inequalities and interpreting monthly payment counts; simple interest supplies the linear model.
questions.methodNote: Form a linear inequality, apply the same operations to both sides and interpret the limiting value in the discrete context, as in Example 2.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Model monthly interest, solve two inequalities and interpret integer payment counts as calendar dates.

classification.difficultyReason: Form a budget inequality with a fixed fee and a per-light cost, then interpret its upper bound as a whole number.

questions.mappingNote: The fixed call-out fee and cost per light produce a two-step budget inequality; the assessed skill is solving and interpreting a linear inequality.
questions.methodNote: Form a linear inequality from the available money, apply the same inverse operations to both sides, and interpret the bound as a whole-number maximum, following Example 2.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Form a budget inequality with a fixed fee and a per-light cost, then interpret its upper bound as a whole number.

classification.difficultyReason: Form an inequality from complementary vote counts, interpret its strict integer bound and justify it graphically.

questions.mappingNote: The central assessed task is modelling and solving a strict linear inequality; line intersection supports the graphical explanation.
questions.methodNote: Use equivalent algebraic operations on inequalities and interpret a non-integral or strict bound using the whole-number context, as in Example 2. Provide the requested graphical comparison as well.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Form an inequality from complementary vote counts, interpret its strict integer bound and justify it graphically.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct two simple-interest balance models and compare them graphically to interpret a strict inequality over time.

questions.mappingNote: Question 14 applies linear balance models and compares their graphs. Simple interest supplies the annual increments; locating the intersection and identifying the graph above the other establishes the required time interval.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 teaches equivalent operations on linear inequations, including reversal when dividing by a negative. Page 3 Example 2 constructs a financial linear expression, solves a threshold inequation and interprets the answer in context.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct two simple-interest balance models and compare them graphically to interpret a strict inequality over time.

classification.difficultyReason: Compare two graphical models of break-even, then form a profit expression and interpret integer solutions to loss and profit inequalities.

questions.mappingNote: Break-even analysis is directly assessed by the two pairs of intersecting linear graphs. The final parts apply the supplied profit model to practical linear inequalities and whole-number sales.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 teaches equivalent operations on inequalities, including reversing the sign for multiplication or division by a negative. Page 3 Example 2 models money remaining with a linear inequality and interprets the result as a whole-number count. Question 15 itself supplies the two graphical break-even methods and defines net profit.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Compare two graphical models of break-even, then form a profit expression and interpret integer solutions to loss and profit inequalities.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply taught operations directly to both interval bounds, preserving endpoint inclusion and reversing inequalities for the negative multiplier.

questions.mappingNote: Each expression is a linear transformation of the given bounded variable, directly applying the inequality operations and double-inequality method on page 2.
questions.methodNote: Apply the same algebraic operation to each member of a double inequality; reverse inequality signs when multiplying or dividing by a negative.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply taught operations directly to both interval bounds, preserving endpoint inclusion and reversing inequalities for the negative multiplier.

classification.difficultyReason: Compare an area upper bound with achievable rectangular packings; the second area bound cannot be attained.

questions.mappingNote: Linear inequalities is the closest supplied skill; rectangular area and spatial packing supply the enrichment context.
questions.methodNote: Use the available area to form a linear inequation, solve it and interpret the whole-number bound, as in the practical computer-purchase example. Then distinguish an area bound from an achievable packing.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Compare an area upper bound with achievable rectangular packings; the second area bound cannot be attained.

classification.difficultyReason: Read strict sign intervals directly from three supplied parabolas with labelled intercepts.

questions.mappingNote: Each item assesses quadratic sign intervals directly from a supplied graph; no algebraic reconstruction is required.
questions.methodNote: Read where the supplied graph lies below or above the x-axis, as taught in Example 3 and the graphical-method summary. Strict inequalities exclude the intercepts.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Read strict sign intervals directly from three supplied parabolas with labelled intercepts.

classification.difficultyReason: Read zeroes and strict positive and negative intervals from supplied quadratic graphs, including an unlabelled origin crossing.

questions.mappingNote: The most advanced directly assessed task is reading quadratic inequality intervals. Part c additionally requires recognising the origin as a zero.
questions.methodNote: Use x-intercepts for y=0 and read where the curve lies above or below the x-axis for strict inequalities, following Example 3 and the graphical-method summary.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Read zeroes and strict positive and negative intervals from supplied quadratic graphs, including an unlabelled origin crossing.

classification.difficultyReason: Read sign regions from three supplied parabolas, include or exclude zeroes appropriately, and confirm each result with test values.

questions.mappingNote: Each a subpart directly assesses the sign of its supplied quadratic graph. Part b independently confirms the same three intervals using tables with values on each side of the zeroes.
questions.methodNote: Example 3 and the graphical-method summary read intervals from where the parabola is positive, zero or negative. Example 4 confirms intervals using zeroes and test values. Example 5 reinforces interval testing; its erroneous intermediate signs in part c are not used.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Read sign regions from three supplied parabolas, include or exclude zeroes appropriately, and confirm each result with test values.

classification.difficultyReason: Sketch six factorised quadratics, select the appropriate sign regions and independently confirm each solution using test values.

questions.mappingNote: Each factorised expression directly supplies two zeroes. Part a requires the concavity and graph sign regions; part b requires a separate confirming table for each expression.
questions.methodNote: Example 3 and the graphical method summary determine solutions from where the associated quadratic is positive, zero or negative. Example 4 confirms signs using test values around the zeroes. Page 8 reinforces the test-point method; its Example 5c contains incorrect intermediate inequality signs, which are not used here.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Sketch six factorised quadratics, select the appropriate sign regions and independently confirm each solution using test values.

classification.difficultyReason: Factorise six quadratics, sketch their parabolas and select the correct sign regions, including endpoints and a downward-opening parabola.

questions.mappingNote: Every part directly assesses quadratic inequalities through factorisation and a parabola sketch. Part f requires downward concavity; parts b, d and e require inclusive endpoints. The erroneous intermediate signs in Example 5c are not used.
questions.methodNote: Factorise to find zeroes, sketch the quadratic, then read where its graph is above, below or on the x-axis. Pages 6–7 explicitly teach this graphical method; page 8 reinforces zeroes and sign regions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Factorise six quadratics, sketch their parabolas and select the correct sign regions, including endpoints and a downward-opening parabola.

classification.difficultyReason: Rearrange and factorise simple quadratic inequalities, interpret sign regions and include repeated-root and strictly positive cases.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts assess quadratic sign regions; parts d and e require recognising a square's non-negative values. The incorrect intermediate signs in Example 5c are not used.
questions.methodNote: Rearrange to compare a quadratic with zero, factorise to locate its zeroes and read the required sign regions from the parabola. Example 3b and Example 4b establish the repeated-root case.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Rearrange and factorise simple quadratic inequalities, interpret sign regions and include repeated-root and strictly positive cases.

classification.difficultyReason: Collect quadratic terms from both sides, factorise and select the appropriate sign regions, including fractional boundaries.

questions.mappingNote: Each part directly assesses quadratic inequations after collecting terms from both sides. Solutions use the taught graphical sign interpretation, with equality included only for non-strict inequalities.
questions.methodNote: Rearrange with zero on one side, factorise to find zeroes, then use the parabola's sign regions. Pages 6–7 teach graphical interpretation and zeroes; page 8 reinforces rearrangement before sign analysis.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Collect quadratic terms from both sides, factorise and select the appropriate sign regions, including fractional boundaries.

classification.difficultyReason: Read solution regions relative to nonzero horizontal levels, then connect the two supplied parabolas through a vertical translation.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and b require comparing the supplied curve with a horizontal level. Part c uses addition of 4 to identify the same inequality on the first supplied graph.
questions.methodNote: Pages 6–7 teach reading quadratic inequality solutions from graphs, including equality at boundary points. Page 8 applies quadratic inequalities in context; its defective Example 5c intermediate signs were not used.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Read solution regions relative to nonzero horizontal levels, then connect the two supplied parabolas through a vertical translation.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct two graphs on one plane and interpret their relative heights to solve a strict quadratic inequality.

questions.mappingNote: Question 9 extends the graphical method to comparing a parabola directly with a line; the solution therefore interprets relative heights rather than replacing the requested method with algebra alone.
questions.methodNote: Pages 6–7 teach reading inequalities from graph heights and treating equality endpoints according to the inequality sign. Page 8 applies quadratic inequalities in context.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct two graphs on one plane and interpret their relative heights to solve a strict quadratic inequality.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate the relative positions of a line and parabola into a strict quadratic inequality, then identify the two exterior solution intervals.

questions.mappingNote: Question 10 requires formulating a quadratic inequation from one graph lying below another, then applying the graphical sign method taught on pages 6–7. Page 8 reinforces translating a condition into an inequation; its Example 5c intermediate sign error is not used.
questions.methodNote: Rearrange the inequation so that one side is zero, find the zeroes, and use the concavity and sign of the associated parabola to select the required intervals.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate the relative positions of a line and parabola into a strict quadratic inequality, then identify the two exterior solution intervals.

classification.difficultyReason: Form a quadratic product model, solve an inclusive inequality using its zeroes and sign, then enumerate distinct integer pairs.

questions.mappingNote: The product is a quadratic in x. Part b uses its boundary zeroes and the sign of an upward-opening parabola; part c restricts the resulting interval to distinct integer pairs.
questions.methodNote: Pages 6–7 teach rearranging a quadratic inequation, finding its zeroes and reading the required sign from its graph or test points. Page 8 applies this method to a contextual quadratic and checks the contextual domain.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Form a quadratic product model, solve an inclusive inequality using its zeroes and sign, then enumerate distinct integer pairs.

classification.difficultyReason: Form an area model from a perimeter, reconcile three metric units and interpret the interval satisfying a strict quadratic inequality.

questions.mappingNote: Part a constructs the rectangle's quadratic area model. Part b directly assesses a quadratic inequality with unit conversion and positive-length restrictions. The incorrect intermediate signs in Example 5c are not used.
questions.methodNote: Rearrange to compare a quadratic with zero, find its zeroes, test its sign in the resulting intervals and apply the physical domain, as in Examples 4 and 5.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Form an area model from a perimeter, reconcile three metric units and interpret the interval satisfying a strict quadratic inequality.

classification.difficultyReason: Model a three-sided fencing constraint, form an area inequality and interpret its single feasible solution as dimensions.

questions.mappingNote: The fencing constraint produces a quadratic area model. Rearrangement gives a non-positive square, matching the double-zero case taught in Examples 3b and 4b; the resulting value must give positive pen dimensions.
questions.methodNote: Pages 6–7 solve quadratic inequations through zeroes and signs, including a squared expression that is non-positive only at its double zero. Example 5 on page 8 models a practical inequality and applies contextual restrictions. Division by a negative reverses the inequality.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Model a three-sided fencing constraint, form an area inequality and interpret its single feasible solution as dimensions.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate a surface-area bound into a quadratic inequality, determine its sign interval and restrict the result to positive radii.

questions.mappingNote: The supplied cylinder formula produces a factorisable quadratic inequality; interpreting its solution for a positive radius is the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Rearrange the quadratic inequality to compare with zero, find its zeroes, use test points to determine signs, and apply the physical domain restriction, following Example 4 and the contextual method in Example 5.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate a surface-area bound into a quadratic inequality, determine its sign interval and restrict the result to positive radii.

classification.difficultyReason: Determine a quadratic's range on two restricted domains, distinguishing an increasing positive interval from an interval containing the vertex.

questions.mappingNote: Question 15 reverses the usual inequality task: use the graph of y=x²+1 to determine its output range on each specified input interval. Part b requires checking the interior vertex rather than merely squaring the endpoints.
questions.methodNote: Pages 6–7 use quadratic graphs to identify positive, zero and negative values, including the vertex; page 8 applies quadratic restrictions in context.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Determine a quadratic's range on two restricted domains, distinguishing an increasing positive interval from an interval containing the vertex.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct a turnover model from direct variation, solve two quadratic inequalities and intersect their solution sets to satisfy both business conditions.

questions.mappingNote: Part a establishes the direct-variation constant, part b constructs the quadratic turnover, part c uses zeroes and test points for the lower turnover bound, and part d repeats that method for the upper bound and intersects the two price sets.
questions.methodNote: Pages 6–7 teach rearranging a quadratic inequality to compare with zero, finding its zeroes and using test points to establish interval signs. Example 5 on page 8 applies this method to a contextual quadratic and intersects with contextual restrictions. The erroneous intermediate signs in Example 5c were not copied.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct a turnover model from direct variation, solve two quadratic inequalities and intersect their solution sets to satisfy both business conditions.

classification.difficultyReason: Derive a quadratic area by subtracting three triangles, solve a repeated-root inequality and establish the area bounds on a restricted domain.

questions.mappingNote: Question 17 requires constructing a quadratic area model, identifying the sole solution of a non-positive square, and completing the square to obtain bounds under geometric restrictions.
questions.methodNote: Page 6 reviews completing the square. Pages 6–7 solve quadratic inequations using graphical signs, including an isolated solution at a double zero. Page 8 models practical quadratic inequations and applies contextual restrictions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Derive a quadratic area by subtracting three triangles, solve a repeated-root inequality and establish the area bounds on a restricted domain.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the sign and perfect-square criteria directly to six supplied discriminants.

questions.mappingNote: Each part supplies a numerical discriminant and asks for existence, rationality and equality of zeroes, directly assessing discriminant-nature-roots.
questions.methodNote: Page 11 gives the sign criteria for the number of real zeroes and the square criterion for rational zeroes when coefficients are rational. Example 6 on page 12 demonstrates combining these criteria; Example 9 on page 13 applies the equal-root and no-real-root conditions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the sign and perfect-square criteria directly to six supplied discriminants.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute numerical coefficients into the discriminant and classify roots by its sign and perfect-square status.

questions.mappingNote: Each part directly assesses numerical evaluation of the discriminant and interpretation of the resulting root count and rationality; discriminant-nature-roots is the closest catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 11 states the sign and square-status tests for the discriminant. Example 6 on page 12 calculates the discriminant and describes rational, double and irrational zeroes without solving. Example 9 on page 13 reinforces the zero and negative discriminant conditions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute numerical coefficients into the discriminant and classify roots by its sign and perfect-square status.

classification.difficultyReason: The instruction supplies the repeated-root condition; each part requires forming the discriminant and solving a linear equation in k.

questions.mappingNote: Every part forms b²−4ac from the given quadratic and solves Δ=0 for k. This directly assesses conditions on a parameter from the discriminant. The returned values in b and d retain a nonzero quadratic coefficient.
questions.methodNote: Page 11 states that a quadratic has one double zero when its discriminant is zero. Example 9(a) on page 13 forms the parameter-dependent discriminant and sets it equal to zero.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: The instruction supplies the repeated-root condition; each part requires forming the discriminant and solving a linear equation in k.

classification.difficultyReason: Form four discriminants linear in a parameter and solve their non-negative conditions.

questions.mappingNote: Each part asks for a parameter range ensuring real roots, directly assessing discriminant-conditions-roots.
questions.methodNote: Page 115 gives the non-negative discriminant condition for real zeroes. Examples 8 and 9 form a parameter-dependent discriminant and solve the required condition. Here each condition is a linear inequality.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Form four discriminants linear in a parameter and solve their non-negative conditions.

classification.difficultyReason: The discriminant condition is supplied; each part requires substitution into the discriminant and solving a linear inequality in the parameter.

questions.mappingNote: Page 11 states the negative-discriminant condition; Examples 8 and 9 on pages 12 and 13 demonstrate parameter conditions. Here each discriminant is linear in the parameter, so direct linear inequality working suffices.
questions.methodNote: Use the discriminant formula and the condition that a quadratic has no real zeroes precisely when its discriminant is negative. Substitute the coefficients, simplify, and solve the resulting parameter inequality.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: The discriminant condition is supplied; each part requires substitution into the discriminant and solving a linear inequality in the parameter.

classification.difficultyReason: Form discriminants with parameter coefficients, expand and factorise quadratic expressions, and solve the repeated-root condition.

questions.mappingNote: Each part directly assesses conditions on an unknown coefficient from a zero discriminant. Parts a and d also require retaining a non-zero quadratic coefficient; the resulting parameter values satisfy this.
questions.methodNote: Use the discriminant formula and the condition that a quadratic has one double zero when its discriminant is zero. Solve the resulting parameter equation, as demonstrated in Example 9(a).

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Form discriminants with parameter coefficients, expand and factorise quadratic expressions, and solve the repeated-root condition.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate a parameter-dependent discriminant, solve its zero condition and reject the value that makes the function constant.

questions.mappingNote: Page 11 states the double-zero condition; Examples 8 and 9 on pages 12–13 demonstrate forming and solving discriminant conditions. This question additionally tests whether the candidate coefficient still defines a parabola.
questions.methodNote: Use Δ=b²−4ac and set Δ=0 for a double zero, solving the resulting parameter equation and retaining a nonzero quadratic coefficient.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate a parameter-dependent discriminant, solve its zero condition and reject the value that makes the function constant.

classification.difficultyReason: Form a discriminant involving a parameter, factorise the resulting quadratic and select the intervals where it is non-negative, including boundary values.

questions.mappingNote: Page 11 states the discriminant conditions. Example 8 on page 12 solves a parameter inequality using test points; Example 9 on page 13 illustrates the equivalent graphical method. All four parts assess these same parameter conditions.
questions.methodNote: Use the condition that real roots require a non-negative discriminant. Calculate and factorise the discriminant, locate its zeroes, and use test points to determine the intervals satisfying the inequality.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Form a discriminant involving a parameter, factorise the resulting quadratic and select the intervals where it is non-negative, including boundary values.

classification.difficultyReason: Form parameter-dependent discriminants and interpret their negative intervals, including a non-negative perfect square with no solution.

questions.mappingNote: Each part assesses parameter conditions for absent x-intercepts. Parts a, b and d use the concavity and zeroes of the discriminant graph; part c uses the non-negativity of a square. These methods agree with the inspected teaching and the individual answer-key graphs.
questions.methodNote: Use Δ=b²−4ac. No real zeroes require Δ<0. Example 9 interprets the negative interval from the graph of Δ against the parameter; Example 8 also supports a table of test points.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Form parameter-dependent discriminants and interpret their negative intervals, including a non-negative perfect square with no solution.

classification.difficultyReason: Prove the three discriminant cases symbolically by completing the square and derive the general formula for the zeroes.

questions.mappingNote: This question proves the nature-of-zeroes results rather than finding parameter ranges. Completing the square and deriving the quadratic formula are supporting skills.
questions.methodNote: Complete the square, set y=0, and use the sign of the discriminant to distinguish no real zeroes, a double zero and two distinct real zeroes. Page 11 supplies Box 4 and the quadratic formula; pages 12–13 demonstrate discriminant conditions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Prove the three discriminant cases symbolically by completing the square and derive the general formula for the zeroes.

classification.difficultyReason: Form an intersection equation, interpret its discriminant and find exact intersection inputs where real solutions exist.

questions.mappingNote: All three responses investigate line–parabola intersections using a suitable quadratic; the discriminant establishes the number of intersections before any roots are calculated.
questions.methodNote: Equate the expressions for y to obtain a quadratic, calculate its discriminant and interpret positive, zero and negative discriminants as two, one and no intersections. Use the quadratic formula for the requested exact x-coordinates, following Box 4 and the substitution approach in Example 7.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Form an intersection equation, interpret its discriminant and find exact intersection inputs where real solutions exist.

classification.difficultyReason: Form a quadratic by equating two parabolas, interpret its discriminant and find exact intersection x-coordinates where real roots exist.

questions.mappingNote: Page 11 supplies the discriminant cases and root formulas; Example 7 on page 12 models reducing simultaneous curve equations to a quadratic and interpreting a double root. Question 12 applies that method to pairs of parabolas.
questions.methodNote: Equate the two expressions for y to obtain a quadratic, calculate its discriminant and use its sign to count real intersections. Use the quadratic formula or the double-root formula to obtain requested x-coordinates.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Form a quadratic by equating two parabolas, interpret its discriminant and find exact intersection x-coordinates where real roots exist.
